prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and import competition reshape labour demand, wages and the regional distribution of employment

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B027 with Autor, Hanson and Katz. Several colleagues' round-1 replies were addressed to my opening two-name Autor-Hanson proposal. My round-1 file already names three, so I restate the position. The reason for the change and the reason it holds is the same. The achievement is a joint account of why labour demand shifts against some workers and places, and where the adjustment lands. The skill-demand and supply framework of Katz and Murphy, and the later work with Autor, gives the long-run wage-structure evidence. As a macroeconomist I use it as the benchmark that capital-skill complementarity is meant to explain. The Autor-Hanson local-labour-market designs give credible evidence on the costs and frictions of adjustment to import competition. Autor appears on both strands, so a single citation worded around labour demand, wages and regional employment is coherent. I have also reconsidered the two-name fallback, which was my own opening proposal. Dropping Katz leaves the technology half resting on Autor alone. Narrowing the citation to import competition would make Dorn's claim at least as strong as Hanson's, so Autor-Hanson would then exclude Dorn without a principle. If the committee narrows the scope, Autor, Dorn and Hanson is the defensible set. A bare two-name award is the weakest of the three versions. The work is mature. Its core papers run from the early 1990s to the mid-2010s and have been replicated, extended and contested, and the critiques have refined magnitudes and persistence more than they have overturned the qualitative findings. I do not treat the nine-file support as merit, and my position rests on the attribution and maturity arguments above.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the main weakness. Dorn, a central co-author of the China-shock papers, is excluded by the three-name limit. The task framework has contributors outside the credited names (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu), and Katz's long-run work is partly adjacent to Goldin's 2023 recognition, so the marginal increment is smaller than the size of the literature suggests. The technology and trade strands use different identification and different co-authors, and a reasonable member could call this two prizes joined by Autor. The size, persistence and external validity of the China-shock effects remain debated, and the papers can be read as strong applied work rather than a conceptual advance. If the committee cannot agree on one citation that states what is new in the Autor-Katz skills framework beyond Acemoglu and Goldin, the case weakens and B012 or B006 should be considered.

responses.point: Friberg moved in round 1 from Autor-Dorn-Hanson to Autor-Hanson-Katz. He argues that a trade-shock-only trio would credit one half of the achievement, and that the citation should be worded around labour demand, wages and local labour markets, not around the task model, to limit the overlap with Acemoglu.
responses.response: I agree with the move and with the wording. The fit between the credited work and the citation is the right test. Your point about wording answers the chair's overlap question better than my opening objection did. The distinct claims are the Katz-Murphy supply-and-demand account of the skill premium and the local-labour-market evidence on import competition. The task model as theory is not one of them. I would add one limit. Because the wording avoids claiming priority for the task model, the committee should say plainly that it is not crediting that theory. Otherwise the citation will be read as a claim over ground that Acemoglu's recognised work partly covers.

responses.point: Teorell prefers Autor, Katz and Hanson. He concedes that Dorn's claim on the trade-shock papers is at least as strong as Hanson's, and says he would support Autor, Dorn and Hanson if the committee narrows the citation to trade exposure. He wants the wording to rest on the empirical demonstration of labour-market effects.
responses.response: This is the clearest statement of the choice, and I accept the conditional. My answer to the chair's question is this. If the committee settles on a trade-adjustment citation, I would accept Autor, Dorn and Hanson over my own set, and I would not defend Autor-Hanson as a fallback. If it wants the joint technology-and-trade citation, Katz is the third name. I read your point that Hanson's co-origination claim is weaker than Dorn's as an argument about scope, not about merit. I would add that the long-run Katz evidence is the part of the package that answers my earlier worry that the shock papers are only applied work. That is the reason I prefer the joint version.

responses.point: Hassler, as chair, prefers B006 with Kiyotaki and Moore alone. He argues that the collateral mechanism is the cleanest macro attribution, is nearly thirty years old, and is distinct from the 2022 prize. He also rejects adding Gertler, because the accelerator lineage was partly recognised in 2022 and Gertler's wider work is better weighed under B018.
responses.response: I accept your Gertler argument and keep to it. A two-name Kiyotaki-Moore award is cleaner than the three-name set I proposed at the opening. I also take your answer on distinctness seriously: the mechanism is a dynamic general-equilibrium propagation channel through asset prices, not a story of runs or intermediation. As a macroeconomist I find that persuasive. On the chair's question, I do not think the thin direct identification is disqualifying. It is a reason to put B006 below a candidate with broadly tested evidence. I have therefore added B006 as an alternative, replacing B032. Its attribution is cleaner than B032's seven-name credit list, and if B027 fails on citation grounds it is a stronger fallback. The reservation that remains is whether the committee wants a second macro-finance award after 2022. Closeness in our own field is a bias risk for both of us, and I flag it.

responses.point: Boppart keeps Katz in B027 because Katz's skill-premium and education-technology work is the older foundation of the literature and fits B027 better than B028. Dropping him would leave the technology half of the citation resting on Autor alone. He would revisit the choice if the citation were limited to the China shock.
responses.response: I now agree. In my round-1 file I changed my position for the same reason, and my opening two-name proposal gave too little weight to the technology half. Katz's role on B028 is a different contribution (the reanalysis of mobility and neighbourhood effects), and it does not reduce his claim here. His appearance on two ballots should not count against him. Your conflict note and mine overlap, because we are frequent co-authors and IIES colleagues. Neither of us has a tie to a credited name, and I treat this as disclosed, not adjudicated. Where I part from you is on the order of fallbacks. I would put B012 ahead of B001 as the first alternative, because the household-debt evidence is younger and the credit-supply debate is still open.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the technology and trade strands as one achievement or two. This decides between Katz and Dorn as the third name, and I would accept Autor, Dorn and Hanson under a trade-adjustment citation.

How far the 2023 (Goldin) and 2024 (Acemoglu) prizes reduce the marginal case for the Autor-Katz skills framework. The citation can avoid claiming the task model, but that does not remove the overlap.
Whether the persistence and external validity of the China-shock effects survive continued reanalysis, and how much of the citation depends on them.
Whether B012 would be a cleaner single-discovery award, once the precursors outside the credited names (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum) and the 2008 trade prize are weighed.
Whether the committee wants a second macro-finance award after 2022, which governs how B006 should be treated as a fallback.
My assessments rely on my own knowledge of the literature and the supplied files, and I have not independently verified any claim.
statement.conflict_note: No personal or co-authorship tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn is apparent from my profile, nor to the credited names in my alternatives (Helpman, Melitz; Kiyotaki, Moore). There is a research adjacency. My own work on capital-skill complementarity and inequality (with Ohanian, Ríos-Rull and Violante) builds on the skill-premium literature that Katz's work anchors, and I may favour that strand. I serve as secretary and have frequent co-authors on the committee, namely Boppart and Hassler (IIES colleagues), and I am a Stockholm University colleague of Teorell. None of these ties involves a credited name in my preferred configuration or alternatives. I disclose them and do not adjudicate them.
